title: Lifetime elision
summary: Three rules let most signatures skip lifetime annotations — until two inputs feed one output.
lecture: You rarely write lifetimes because the compiler fills them in by three elision rules: (1) each elided input reference gets its own fresh lifetime; (2) if there is exactly one input lifetime, the output gets it; (3) in methods, &self's lifetime goes to the output.

Elision fails exactly where our lifetime puzzles live: two borrowed inputs and a borrowed output. Rule 1 gives a and b different lifetimes, rule 2 doesn't apply, and the compiler cannot guess which input the result borrows from — E0106, 'missing lifetime specifier'.
That error is not the compiler being pedantic. The answer genuinely isn't in the signature; you add <'a> to write it down. Understanding WHICH rule failed tells you exactly what to annotate.

example.caption: One input elides cleanly; two inputs need an explicit 'a.
